articles.title: Extreme heat is making pesticides more dangerous for US farmworkers, report warns - The Cool Down

articles.full_text:
As temperatures climb across U.S. farm country, a dangerous overlap is coming into sharp focus: Extreme heat can make pesticide exposure even more harmful for the people harvesting the nation's food.
Inside Climate News reported that researchers and farmworker advocates see this as a growing danger for the country's 2.4 million farmworkers.
Here's what to know
Researchers say hot weather can change both workers' bodies and the chemicals around them. Beyond making farm labor more physically taxing, high temperatures can increase sweating and skin absorption, speed pesticide evaporation, and in some cases alter chemicals into more toxic forms.
Exposure can happen through more than one route, Omanjana Goswami of the Union for Concerned Scientists' food and environmental program said.
"When it's in the air, you are inhaling it through your nose. You are exposed to it through your other organs like skin," Goswami told ICN. "Your skin can absorb some of the pesticides [that are] in the air, and also when you're sweating as part of doing your work you are increasing the pore size of your skin. It is awful. There is no other word for it."
Reported poisonings are not limited to people who spray pesticides; field workers account for most documented cases. A Union for Concerned Scientists report found that acute pesticide poisoning affects thousands of U.S. farmworkers each year, though many incidents are believed to go unreported.
Over the long term, pesticide exposure has been linked to cancer, depression, diabetes, neurodegenerative diseases, and reproductive problems.
More background
When heat stress and pesticide exposure happen at the same time, the odds of immediate illness can rise. Risk can also follow workers home because residue left on skin or clothing may expose others.
Jeannie Economos, the pesticide safety and environmental health project coordinator at the Farmworker Association of Florida, said the burden falls on people with the least power to avoid it.
"This is definitely a case of environmental injustice," she told ICN.
Most U.S. farmworkers are immigrants and people of color. Economos described them as "landless farmers," saying that immigration status, lack of capital, and discriminatory systems leave many workers especially vulnerable.
Heat is the leading weather-related killer in the United States. Citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration said 1,042 workers died of heat-related causes from 1992 to 2022 — about 34 per year, ICN reported.
What's being done?
OSHA is advancing a heat standard it proposed in 2024. The rule would more clearly define employer obligations and require companies to identify and address heat hazards on the job.
Because no dedicated federal standard exists, OSHA has relied on the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970's general duty clause. That provision requires employers to keep workplaces free of known dangers that could seriously injure or kill workers.
Several states — California, Colorado, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington — have heat protections. Some states, including Texas and Florida, have blocked cities or counties from adopting similar rules. In 2024, Florida lawmakers stopped local governments from setting outdoor worker heat standards after Miami-Dade County considered a measure that would have required water breaks, rest breaks, and training on heat illness.
"We tell people, don't pick up your children when you get home until you take your clothes off and take a shower, because you're going to contaminate your kids," Economos said, according to ICN.
Where can I learn more?
The problem doesn't end with one field or one shift. Rising temperatures, uneven protections, and pesticide exposure can put farmworkers and nearby communities at risk.
• Across hotter regions, less obvious heat harms are sending more people to hospitals.
• Consumer Reports found harmful pesticide residues linger on many popular fruits and vegetables.
These stories add context to the ways heat and chemical exposure can stack up for workers, families, and neighbors. They also help explain why stronger protections matter all along the food chain.

JCPS implementing safety measures for athletes due to heat advisory
Outdoor activities are cancelled for Wednesday and Thursday, with activities on other days subject to rescheduling or moving indoors.
Outdoor activities are cancelled for Wednesday and Thursday, with activities on other days subject to rescheduling or moving indoors.
Jefferson County Public Schools is canceling outdoor practices and competitions Wednesday and Thursday because of a forecasted heat advisory, and officials say schedules may be affected all week.
April Brooks, who oversees athletics and activities for JCPS, said the district is taking no chances and is also rescheduling activities on other days to keep student-athletes out of the worst of the heat.
“With it being a heat advisory coming up this week, we thought we really needed to take some precautionary measures,” Brooks said. “We’re just looking at those 100-degree temperatures and saying we’re probably going to get close to that or near that, and so I’d rather be on the side of caution.”
This includes Friday night football competitions.
“You might see the games are pushed back — 7:30-8 p.m. — just to get away from the high heat,” Brooks said.
The district and the KHSAA rely on wet-bulb globe temperature measurements, which factor in temperature, humidity, wind, sun and clouds.
Dr. Victor Kremser of Norton Sports Health said humidity is a major concern.
“Humidity stops the sweat from evaporating, and then you get the heat trapped in your body, and then the core temperature rises,” Kremser said.
Kremser said rising core temperature can lead to heat exhaustion, with symptoms including cramping, heavy sweating, nausea, vomiting, fatigue and excessive thirst.
If sweating stops or an athlete appears confused, he said those are signs of possible heatstroke.
“Rapid cooling down has to happen as soon as possible — and actually we have to do that before we transfer the athlete to the hospital,” Kremser said.
Brooks said district trainers and coaches are trained to recognize and prevent heat exhaustion.
“We have cooling tubs, ice towels. We have water, constantly shaded areas that we’re taking those breaks,” Brooks said.
She also said fans need to take precautions.
“Even if you’re sitting in the heat and you haven’t hydrated, well, they also can have heat illness as well,” Brooks said.

articles.full_text:
Allegheny County officials are issuing a Code Red Heat Advisory because of multiple days of extreme heat.
The advisory goes into effect on Tuesday and stays in place through Thursday.
Channel 11 meteorologists say temperatures will hit the lower 90s for much of the week ahead, with humidity making it feel even warmer. Allegheny County officials say the conditions may pose a risk to vulnerable residents.
During the intense heat, cooling centers will be open throughout the county. You can find the cooling center nearest you by clicking here or calling 211.
While the advisory is in place, the Allegheny County Department of Human Services will check on older adults and street outreach teams will connect with those experiencing unsheltered homelessness to provide water and cooling supplies.
Everyone is encouraged to check on their neighbors, friends and families.
Allegheny County Emergency Services provided the following heat safety reminders:
- Check on your elderly neighbors or those without air conditioning
Symptoms of heat exhaustion to monitor for include dizziness, nausea, headache or excessive sweating. If you experience any of these, take a break and find a place to cool down. If they continue, seek help.
